title: Temples in the West
hookLine: Japanese American temples, including through the wartime internment camps where practice continued

cards: A Sunday morning in a plain wooden barracks. Benches in rows. A small altar built by hand, an incense bowl, a priest in robes, and families chanting together.
Outside the door: a fence, and a guard tower. During the Second World War, the United States government forced Japanese Americans from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps.
Among the things people carried in with them was their Buddhist practice. Inside the fence, it kept going.

teach.b: Japanese families who settled in Hawaii and on the American mainland built temples, among them temples of Jodo Shinshu, the Pure Land school of Shinran we met in Japan.
These were family temples: services, funerals, Sunday schools for the children, and the summer Obon festival, when the dead are remembered and the community dances together in the street.
When war came between the United States and Japan, Buddhist priests, as community leaders, were among those taken away for questioning and detention.
Then whole families, citizens and not, were removed to camps in the interior. Temples were closed, and some families hid or left behind their home altars.
In the camps, people organized Buddhist services, held funerals, ran Sunday schools and youth groups, and danced Obon in the dust between the barracks.
They said the nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, entrusting themselves to Amida Buddha.
At a camp in Utah, during those years, the mainland temple association took the name Buddhist Churches of America, and it still goes by that name.
After the camps closed, families came home, reopened temples, and started again.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, has a picture of steadiness that fits: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise."
Wind on every side, and with their temples shut, the communities kept their ground.

how: Japanese American Buddhist temples, including Jodo Shinshu temples, hold regular services, Sunday schools and a summer Obon festival with dancing, and some communities hold pilgrimages to the sites of the wartime camps.

practice: Bring to mind a community that came through something hard and kept its practices going: these families behind a fence, or your own family, a neighborhood, a congregation, a group of friends.
Hold them in mind without needing to say anything; if you like, bow your head or put your palms together for a moment. Then sit quietly with them.
